The Case for American Acquisition of Greenland: Strategic Imperative of the 21st Century

Introduction

In an era defined by great-power competition, melting Arctic ice, and the relentless pursuit of critical resources, few geopolitical opportunities rival the strategic potential of Greenland. The world's largest island — vast, resource-rich, sparsely populated, and geographically positioned at the crossroads of the Atlantic and Arctic — represents a once-in-a-century opportunity for the United States to secure its national interests for generations to come. While the notion of acquiring Greenland may seem audacious to some, a clear-eyed examination of America's strategic needs, the island's extraordinary resource potential, and the shifting global order reveals that actively pursuing this acquisition is not merely desirable — it is an imperative the United States can ill afford to ignore.

I. The Geographic and Military Strategic Case

A. The Arctic Is the New Center of Gravity

The Arctic is rapidly transforming from a frozen afterthought into one of the most consequential theaters of global competition. As climate change accelerates the retreat of polar ice, new shipping lanes are opening — most notably the Northern Sea Route along Russia's coast and the Northwest Passage through the Canadian Arctic. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has documented that Arctic sea ice extent has declined by roughly 13% per decade since satellite monitoring began. By mid-century, the Arctic Ocean may experience virtually ice-free summers, opening transit routes that could reduce shipping times between Europe and Asia by up to 40%.

This is not a distant hypothetical. It is happening now, and the nations that position themselves early will reap enormous advantages. Russia has been aggressively militarizing its Arctic coastline, constructing new military bases, deploying hypersonic missiles, and building a fleet of nuclear-powered icebreakers. China, despite having no Arctic coastline, has declared itself a "near-Arctic state" and has invested billions in Arctic infrastructure, research stations, and partnerships with Nordic nations.

Greenland sits at the geographic epicenter of this transformation. Its position — bridging North America and Europe, commanding approaches to the North Atlantic, and straddling emerging Arctic transit routes — makes it one of the most strategically valuable landmasses on Earth. Whoever controls or has unchallenged access to Greenland holds a commanding position over the Arctic's future.

B. Thule Air Base and the Arctic Defense Perimeter

The United States already maintains a significant military presence in Greenland through Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base), the Department of Defense's northernmost installation. This base is a critical node in America's early warning and space surveillance architecture, housing radar systems that detect intercontinental ballistic missile launches and tracking satellites in polar orbit. It has been a cornerstone of U.S. and NATO Arctic defense since the Cold War.

However, America's current arrangement rests on a lease agreement with Denmark — a nation of fewer than six million people whose military budget and capability are modest by global standards. Denmark's sovereignty over Greenland means that any expansion of U.S. facilities, any new deployment, or any enhanced mission set requires Danish approval and is subject to Danish domestic politics. In a crisis — particularly one involving Chinese or Russian encroachment in the Arctic — this dependency introduces an unacceptable level of uncertainty.

Acquisition would eliminate this vulnerability. The United States would have the sovereign authority to develop Greenland's military infrastructure without diplomatic intermediaries, rapidly expanding bases, deploying advanced missile defense systems, stationing naval assets, and establishing Arctic training facilities. Greenland could become the anchor of a comprehensive Arctic defense perimeter, complementing existing assets in Alaska and ensuring total dominance of the northern approaches to the North American continent.

C. Control of the GIUK Gap

Greenland's strategic importance extends beyond the Arctic. The island is central to controlling the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom (GIUK) gap — the maritime chokepoint through which Russian naval vessels, particularly submarines, must pass to reach the open Atlantic. During the Cold War, controlling this gap was a central pillar of NATO's strategy to prevent Soviet submarines from threatening transatlantic supply lines.

That mission has returned with urgency. Russia's submarine fleet has been modernized and expanded. Its new Yasen-class attack submarines and Borei-class ballistic missile submarines are quieter, more capable, and more numerous than their Soviet predecessors. NATO commanders have repeatedly warned that Russian submarine activity in the North Atlantic has returned to Cold War levels. Controlling the GIUK gap from a sovereign American position in Greenland would provide an irreplaceable advantage in any naval confrontation.

II. The Resource and Economic Case

A. Critical Minerals for the Future Economy

Beneath Greenland's ice sheet and along its exposed bedrock lies one of the world's most significant deposits of rare earth elements (REEs) and critical minerals. Rare earth elements — a group of 17 metallic elements — are essential to the production of smartphones, electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, advanced weapons systems, and countless other technologies that define the modern economy and the modern military.

Today, China dominates global rare earth production, controlling approximately 60% of mining output and an even more staggering 90% of processing and refining capacity. This monopoly represents a profound strategic vulnerability. Beijing has demonstrated its willingness to weaponize this dominance — most notably during a 2010 diplomatic dispute with Japan, when China imposed an unofficial rare earth export ban, sending global prices soaring and sending shockwaves through supply chains worldwide.

Greenland's subsoil contains substantial deposits of rare earth elements, along with significant quantities of uranium, zinc, iron ore, copper, and other minerals critical to the green energy transition and advanced manufacturing. A 2021 survey by the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland confirmed that Greenland's mineral potential is vast and largely untapped. Under American stewardship, these resources could be developed responsibly and strategically, breaking China's chokehold on critical mineral supply chains and securing American economic independence for decades.

B. Energy Resources

The waters surrounding Greenland are believed to contain substantial hydrocarbon reserves. Surveys by the U.S. Geological Survey have estimated that the Arctic as a whole may hold approximately 90 billion barrels of undiscovered oil and 1,669 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Greenland's offshore basins, particularly along its western and eastern coasts, are considered prospective for significant oil and gas deposits.

While the transition to renewable energy is a global priority, the reality is that oil and gas will remain essential components of the global energy mix for decades to come. Securing access to these reserves under American sovereignty would enhance U.S. energy security, reduce dependence on volatile Middle Eastern markets, and provide strategic reserves that could prove decisive in any future global supply disruption.

C. Freshwater and the Ice Sheet Itself

Greenland's ice sheet contains approximately 2.85 million cubic kilometers of ice — enough fresh water, if fully melted, to raise global sea levels by roughly 7.4 meters. While no one advocates for melting the ice sheet, the reality of climate change means that its gradual contribution to rising seas will have enormous global consequences.

Whoever governs Greenland will have a seat at the table — arguably the head of the table — in negotiations over global water resources, sea-level rise adaptation, and climate policy. As freshwater scarcity becomes an increasingly urgent global challenge, sovereignty over the world's second-largest ice mass would confer extraordinary leverage and influence.

III. The Geopolitical and Geoeconomic Case

A. Denying Greenland to Strategic Competitors

The most urgent argument for American acquisition may be the simplest: preventing anyone else from gaining a dominant foothold. China has aggressively pursued economic and infrastructure partnerships across the Arctic, including attempts to finance and build airports and mining operations in Greenland itself. In 2018, a Chinese state-owned enterprise attempted to finance the construction of three airports in Greenland — a move that alarmed both Copenhagen and Washington and was ultimately blocked under U.S. pressure.

China's strategy is clear: use economic investment to establish presence, then leverage that presence for strategic advantage. The "Polar Silk Road," China's Arctic component of its Belt and Road Initiative, envisions Chinese-built infrastructure, Chinese-funded ports, and Chinese economic dependency across the Arctic. If Denmark — a small nation with limited resources to invest in Greenland's development — cannot or will not counter Chinese economic penetration, then the logical alternative is for the United States to assume direct responsibility.

American acquisition would slam the door on Chinese and Russian ambitions in the region, permanently anchoring Greenland within the Western security architecture and ensuring that its development serves Western strategic interests.

B. Strengthening the Western Alliance

Some may object that pursuing Greenland would damage the U.S.-Denmark relationship. This concern, while understandable, overstates the risk. Denmark is a NATO ally and a close partner, but it is also a nation that has historically struggled to invest adequately in Greenland's development and defense. The approximately 56,000 people who live in Greenland face significant challenges — economic underdevelopment, limited infrastructure, high unemployment, and a dependence on Danish subsidies that has not translated into prosperity.

An American commitment to Greenland — backed by the resources of the world's largest economy — could transform the island's prospects. Investment in infrastructure, education, healthcare, and sustainable economic development could dramatically improve the quality of life for Greenland's residents. Military investment would create jobs and economic activity. If structured as a consensual arrangement — perhaps through a compact of free association similar to those the U.S. maintains with the Marshall Islands, Palau, and the Federated States of Micronesia — the transition could be mutually beneficial and broadly supported.

Moreover, in an era when NATO allies are being called upon to increase defense spending and share the burden of collective security, Denmark's contribution of Greenland to the Western strategic architecture could be framed as a meaningful contribution to the alliance — one that aligns with the broader NATO commitment to Arctic security.

C. The Monroe Doctrine's Modern Application

The United States has a long historical tradition of opposing European colonial possessions in the Western Hemisphere. The Monroe Doctrine, articulated in 1823, established the principle that the Americas are not a theater for European territorial expansion. While the world has changed enormously since the 19th century, the fundamental logic of the Monroe Doctrine — that major powers should not maintain colonial possessions in the Western Hemisphere that could serve as staging grounds for rival great powers — retains relevance.

Greenland is geographically part of the North American continent. It is separated from Canada by mere kilometers and lies far closer to New York than to Copenhagen. Its inclusion within the Danish realm is a historical artifact of medieval Norse colonization, not a reflection of geographic, cultural, or strategic logic. The people of Greenland are Inuit — culturally and ethnically connected to the indigenous peoples of Canada, Alaska, and the broader Arctic, not to Scandinavia. Bringing Greenland into a closer relationship with the United States would, in many ways, be a reuniting of the Arctic peoples of North America.

IV. The Will of Greenland's People

Any discussion of Greenland's political future must center the aspirations of its people. The approximately 56,000 residents of Greenland — the vast majority of whom are Inuit — have been on a long trajectory toward greater autonomy and, ultimately, independence. Greenland achieved home rule in 1979 and expanded self-government in 2009. A 2021 survey found that a majority of Greenlanders support eventual independence from Denmark, but many also recognize the economic challenges of full sovereignty — the island currently depends on an annual Danish block grant of approximately $500 million, which constitutes roughly one-third of the government's budget.

The United States could offer Greenland a path that combines political autonomy with economic vitality. A compact of free association would allow Greenland to maintain self-governance over domestic affairs while benefiting from American military protection, economic investment, and access to the world's largest market. Greenlanders could retain their language, culture, and traditions while gaining access to opportunities that Denmark's limited resources cannot provide.

The U.S. has successfully managed such arrangements before. The freely associated states of the Pacific — the Marshall Islands, Palau, and the Federated States of Micronesia — have maintained their cultural identities and domestic self-governance while benefiting enormously from their association with the United States. A similar model could be adapted for Greenland, respecting Inuit sovereignty while addressing the strategic and economic realities of the 21st century.

V. Addressing Objections

"This Is Colonialism"

Acquisition does not mean colonialism. The entire premise of any arrangement must be the free, informed, and enthusiastic consent of the Greenlandic people. Colonialism is characterized by exploitation, cultural erasure, and the denial of political rights. An American compact with Greenland would, by definition, require the opposite: investment, cultural respect, and the enhancement of political autonomy. The goal is not to impose American rule on unwilling people, but to offer a partnership that serves mutual interests.

"Denmark Would Never Agree"

Denmark is a sovereign nation with the legal authority over Greenland's external affairs, and any arrangement would require Danish cooperation. However, Denmark's relationship with Greenland is not without its own tensions. The legacy of colonial-era policies, the Thule forced relocation controversy, and ongoing debates about the adequacy of Danish investment have created friction. A well-structured arrangement — one that includes generous financial compensation to Denmark, continued cultural and educational ties between Denmark and Greenland, and the explicit consent of the Greenlandic people — could be framed in a way that serves Danish interests as well, including by strengthening the broader Western security architecture of which Denmark is a part.

"The Cost Would Be Enormous"

Greenland is not an uninhabited wilderness — but it is very sparsely populated and very large (over 2.1 million square kilometers). The costs of investment would be significant but manageable for the United States, particularly when weighed against the strategic dividends. The U.S. currently spends over $800 billion annually on defense; the incremental cost of developing Greenland's military infrastructure would be a fraction of that figure. Economic investments in resource development and infrastructure could generate returns that far exceed the initial outlay. And the long-term cost of not securing Greenland — of allowing it to become a vector for Chinese or Russian influence, or of failing to develop its critical mineral resources — is far greater.

Conclusion

The acquisition of Greenland is not a fanciful notion — it is a strategic necessity rooted in geography, resources, and the realities of 21st-century great-power competition. The Arctic is opening, and with it a new frontier of competition between the United States, China, and Russia. Greenland sits at the center of this frontier — geographically, militarily, and economically. Its critical mineral deposits offer a path to breaking free of dangerous supply chain dependencies. Its military geography is irreplaceable. And its people deserve an economic partnership that can deliver the prosperity and autonomy they seek.

The United States has a history of bold territorial decisions that, at the time, seemed controversial but proved transformative — the Louisiana Purchase, the acquisition of Alaska, the Marshall Islands compacts. Greenland is the Alaska of the 21st century: dismissed by some as a frozen wasteland, but destined to prove its incalculable value as the world changes around it. The question is not whether Greenland will be strategically consequential. The question is whether the United States will have the vision and the will to secure its future there. The answer must be yes.

Geological surveys have identified massive deposits of rare earth elements, including neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium—materials essential for modern technology, renewable energy systems, and defense applications. In the great power competition of the 21st century, geography remains destiny. Russia has aggressively expanded its Arctic presence, building new bases and claiming vast swaths of Arctic seafloor. Introduction

For decades, Greenland—a vast, sparsely populated territory in the Arctic—has been a geopolitical curiosity rather than a strategic necessity. The Arctic is no longer a frozen backwater but the epicenter of a new great-power competition. With diplomatic skill, economic incentives, and a clear vision of American leadership, the U.S. can acquire Greenland without war, without scandal, and with overwhelming strategic benefit.

The Case for American Acquisition of Greenland: A Strategic Imperative for the 21st Century

Introduction

In 1867, Secretary of State William Seward was mercilessly mocked for purchasing Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million—a transaction derided as "Seward's Folly." Today, Alaska stands as one of the most strategically vital and resource-rich territories in the American portfolio, a testament to the vision of leaders willing to think in generational terms rather than news cycles. The United States now faces a comparable opportunity—one that may prove even more consequential for the trajectory of American power in the coming century: the acquisition of Greenland.

The idea is neither frivolous nor unprecedented. President Harry Truman formally offered Denmark $100 million for Greenland in 1946. The United States has maintained a significant military presence on the island since World War II. Multiple administrations have explored the concept, and the underlying logic has only strengthened as the Arctic has emerged as the next great theater of geopolitical competition. The acquisition of Greenland—pursued through respectful negotiation, generous compensation, and with due regard for the rights and aspirations of its people—would represent the single most important strategic move the United States could make to secure its interests for the remainder of the 21st century.

This essay argues that the acquisition of Greenland is justified and advisable on three reinforcing grounds: its unparalleled geostrategic position in an era of Arctic competition, its extraordinary endowment of natural resources critical to American economic and technological independence, and its capacity to reshape the geopolitical balance of power decisively in America's favor.

I. The Arctic Chessboard: Greenland's Geostrategic Supremacy

A. The Opening of the Arctic

Climate change, whatever its broader consequences, is producing one undeniable geopolitical reality: the Arctic is opening. Summer sea ice has declined by approximately 40% since satellite measurements began in 1979, and many scientists project ice-free Arctic summers within the coming decades. This transformation is converting the Arctic Ocean from an impassable barrier into a navigable waterway—and with navigability comes competition.

New shipping lanes, particularly the Northern Sea Route along Russia's coast and the hypothetical Transpolar Sea Route directly across the pole, promise to shorten transit times between Asia and Europe by thousands of miles. The Arctic seabed is believed to contain roughly 13% of the world's undiscovered oil reserves and 30% of its undiscovered natural gas, according to the United States Geological Survey. Where resources and trade routes converge, great power competition inevitably follows.

Greenland sits at the geographic and strategic heart of this emerging theater. The world's largest island—spanning over 836,000 square miles—commands the approaches between the North Atlantic and the Arctic Ocean. It flanks the passages connecting the Arctic to European waters and overlooks the corridors through which any major naval or commercial transit must pass. In the great power competition that will define this century, controlling Greenland is the equivalent of controlling the high ground.

B. Countering Russian Ambitions

Russia has invested more aggressively in Arctic capabilities than any other nation. Moscow has reactivated and expanded Soviet-era military bases across its northern coastline, established new Arctic brigade combat teams, deployed advanced missile defense systems above the Arctic Circle, and built the world's largest fleet of icebreakers—including nuclear-powered vessels that no other nation can match. Russia's Northern Fleet, headquartered in Murmansk, represents one of the most powerful naval concentrations on Earth.

Russia's Arctic strategy is not defensive. Moscow has made explicit claims to vast swaths of the Arctic seabed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, planted a titanium flag on the ocean floor beneath the North Pole, and repeatedly used military exercises to signal its willingness to enforce those claims. Russia views the Arctic as both an economic lifeline—hydrocarbons from Arctic fields account for a significant share of Russian state revenue—and a strategic frontier where it can project power and challenge Western dominance.

American acquisition of Greenland would fundamentally alter this equation. It would extend the American defensive perimeter deep into the Arctic, provide basing options for naval and air assets capable of monitoring and countering Russian movements, and ensure that the Western alliance maintains a credible presence in a region where Russia currently enjoys significant geographic advantages. The existing Pituffik Space Base (formerly Thule Air Base) in northwestern Greenland already provides critical ballistic missile early warning and satellite tracking capabilities. Full sovereignty over Greenland would allow the United States to expand and modernize this infrastructure without the diplomatic constraints inherent in operating on foreign soil.

C. Confronting China's Arctic Aspirations

Perhaps even more alarming than Russian militarization is China's increasingly assertive Arctic strategy. Despite having no territory above the Arctic Circle, Beijing declared itself a "Near-Arctic State" in its 2018 Arctic policy white paper and has pursued what it calls a "Polar Silk Road" as an extension of its Belt and Road Initiative. China has invested billions in Arctic infrastructure projects, cultivated diplomatic relationships with Arctic nations, and built a growing fleet of research icebreakers with obvious dual-use potential.

China's interest in Greenland specifically has been direct and concerning. Chinese state-backed firms have pursued mining contracts and infrastructure projects on the island, including a bid to build international airports—projects that would have given Beijing a strategic foothold within the Western hemisphere's Arctic approaches. The Danish government, to its credit, blocked several of these initiatives, recognizing the security implications. But Denmark, a nation of fewer than six million people with a modest defense budget, cannot be expected to serve as the permanent bulwark against Chinese encroachment in one of the most strategically important territories on Earth.

American sovereignty over Greenland would definitively close this vulnerability. It would eliminate the possibility of Chinese economic leverage evolving into strategic influence, remove a potential target of Beijing's proven strategy of debt-trap diplomacy, and send an unmistakable signal that the Arctic's Western flank is not available for great power bargaining.

D. The GIUK Gap and North Atlantic Defense

Military strategists have long recognized the critical importance of the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom (GIUK) Gap—the series of maritime chokepoints through which Russian naval forces must pass to access the Atlantic Ocean. During the Cold War, monitoring and controlling these passages was a cornerstone of NATO strategy, and its importance has only grown as Russia has modernized its submarine fleet, including new classes of ballistic missile submarines and advanced attack submarines that challenge Western detection capabilities.

Greenland forms the western anchor of this defensive line. American sovereignty over the island would transform the GIUK Gap from a line that must be cooperatively defended into one where the United States controls two of the three anchor points (Greenland and, through close alliance, effective coordination with Iceland and the UK). This would provide unmatched flexibility in deploying undersea surveillance networks, anti-submarine warfare assets, and naval forces to counter any Russian attempt to break into the Atlantic—a scenario that remains central to NATO contingency planning.

Beneath Greenland's ice sheet and across its exposed coastal regions lies what may be the most strategically significant concentration of critical minerals in the Western world. Geological surveys have identified substantial deposits of rare earth elements (REEs)—the group of 17 metallic elements that are indispensable to modern technology, from smartphones and electric vehicles to precision-guided munitions and advanced fighter aircraft.

Currently, China dominates global rare earth production, controlling approximately 60-70% of mining output and an even larger share of processing capacity. Bringing these resources under American sovereignty would represent a generational step toward breaking China's stranglehold on critical mineral supply chains, securing the inputs necessary for the clean energy transition, and ensuring that America's defense industry is never dependent on an adversary for essential materials.

B. Hydrocarbons and Energy Security

The waters surrounding Greenland are believed to hold substantial oil and natural gas reserves. The USGS has estimated that the broader Arctic region contains approximately 90 billion barrels of undiscovered oil and 1,669 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Greenland's offshore basins—particularly along its western and northeastern coasts—are among the most promising unexplored hydrocarbon frontiers in the world.

While the global energy landscape is evolving, hydrocarbons will remain essential to the American and global economy for decades. Greenland's ice sheet contains approximately 10% of the world's total freshwater reserves—roughly 680,000 cubic miles of frozen fresh water. As climate change intensifies water scarcity across much of the globe, freshwater is increasingly recognized as a strategic resource of the first order. While the practical challenges of harvesting and transporting Arctic freshwater are significant, ongoing advances in desalination, water treatment, and transportation technology may eventually make Greenland's freshwater reserves an asset of incalculable value.

Securing sovereign control over this resource now—before water scarcity becomes an acute global crisis—represents the kind of forward-looking strategic investment that distinguishes great powers from ordinary nations.

D. Fisheries and Maritime Resources

Greenland's surrounding waters support some of the richest fisheries in the North Atlantic. Shrimp, halibut, cod, and other species thrive in these cold, nutrient-rich waters. As global fish stocks face increasing pressure from overfishing and climate-driven ecosystem changes, Arctic and sub-Arctic fisheries are expected to grow in productivity and importance. American sovereignty over Greenland would extend U.S. exclusive economic zone (EEZ) claims over vast areas of productive ocean, dramatically expanding America's maritime resource base and providing leverage in international fisheries negotiations.

III. Geopolitical Transformation: Reshaping the Balance of Power

A. Expanding American Sovereignty and Territorial Reach

The acquisition of Greenland would represent the largest territorial expansion of the United States since the Alaska Purchase—and potentially the most consequential since the Louisiana Purchase. It would make the United States the dominant territorial power in the Arctic, extending American sovereignty across a landmass larger than Mexico and an EEZ encompassing hundreds of thousands of additional square miles of ocean.

This expansion would carry profound implications for America's voice in Arctic governance. Currently, the United States is one of eight members of the Arctic Council, but its Arctic coastline is limited to Alaska. Adding Greenland would give the United States a second major Arctic coast, enhance its claims and standing in Arctic territorial and resource disputes, and fundamentally reshape the balance of influence within Arctic institutions. America would transition from being one Arctic power among several to being the preeminent Arctic nation—a status commensurate with its global role.

Critics may argue that acquiring Greenland from Denmark could strain alliance relationships. In reality, a well-negotiated acquisition could strengthen the Western security architecture. Denmark, despite its admirable commitment to the alliance, faces genuine challenges in defending and developing Greenland. The island's population of approximately 56,000 is spread across a territory larger than Western Europe, with limited infrastructure, no road system connecting settlements, and a defense posture that depends almost entirely on Danish military assets that are already stretched thin by European security commitments.

A generous acquisition—one that includes substantial financial compensation, continued cultural protections for Greenland's Indigenous Inuit population, infrastructure investment, and perhaps preferential trade arrangements—could relieve Denmark of a defense burden it struggles to sustain while providing resources that Copenhagen could redirect toward European defense. Any acquisition must, of course, address the rights and aspirations of Greenland's population. Indeed, if the United States were to invest even a fraction of what it spends on overseas military operations into developing Greenland's infrastructure and social services, it could transform the island's standard of living within a generation—something that decades of Danish subsidies have not fully achieved.

Greenland is one of the most important scientific research sites on Earth. Its ice sheet provides an unparalleled record of climate history, its ecosystems offer insights into Arctic ecology and the effects of climate change, and its geology informs our understanding of planetary processes. American sovereignty would enable the United States to dramatically expand scientific research on the island, positioning itself as the global leader in Arctic and climate science.

Any purchase price must be measured against the alternative costs of not acquiring Greenland: decades of escalating military expenditures to project power into the Arctic from distant bases, vulnerability to Chinese mineral supply chain manipulation, and the strategic consequences of allowing an adversary to establish influence in a region vital to American security. Climate shifts are opening new shipping lanes that will reshape global commerce. The Northern Sea Route and the Northwest Passage are becoming navigable for longer seasons each year. Greenland is not merely strategic real estate — it is a treasure vault.

Beneath its ice sheet and within its exposed bedrock lie some of the most significant deposits of rare earth elements on the planet. This is not fantasy. This is achievable. It requires only what every great American undertaking has required: vision, will, and the courage to act.

My fellow Americans —

Jefferson had the vision to look west. Seward had the courage to look north. Now it falls to our generation to look to the Arctic — to the vast, magnificent, resource-rich island of Greenland — and to declare that America's future will not be written by timidity.

Imagine a scenario where Russian or Chinese vessels freely traverse the Northwest Passage without U.S. oversight; acquiring Greenland prevents this dystopia, transforming a potential vulnerability into an impregnable fortress.
